source_excerpts: Let $\mathbb S^2=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:|x|=1\}$ with its usual surface-area measure $dS$, normalized so $\int_{\mathbb S^2}dS=4\pi$. For an integer $\ell\ge0$, let $\mathcal H_\ell$ be the complex vector space of restrictions to $\mathbb S^2$ of homogeneous degree-$\ell$ polynomials $P(x_1,x_2,x_3)$ satisfying $\Delta P=0$. Give $\mathcal H_\ell$ the inner product $\langle f,g\rangle=\int_{\mathbb S^2}f\overline g\,dS$, linear in the first argument. An orthonormal basis is not fixed by this definition; the addition-theorem item proves that $\dim\mathcal H_\ell=2\ell+1$ and that such a finite basis exists.

If $Y_{\ell m}\in\mathcal H_\ell$ is later chosen from an orthonormal basis and $v\ne0$, its associated homogeneous harmonic polynomial is $H_{\ell m}(v)=|v|^\ell Y_{\ell m}(v/|v|)$. At $v=0$ use the polynomial value: $H_{00}(0)=Y_{00}$ and $H_{\ell m}(0)=0$ for $\ell>0$. This is the regular-solid-harmonic convention used in the 3D evaluator.

source_excerpts: Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open. Write $B(x,r)$ for the open Euclidean ball from [[def-metric-ball]] with distance induced by [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. A family of cells is **locally finite** here when every compact subset of $\Omega$ meets only finitely many cells. A bounded set is **Jordan measurable** when its Jordan inner and outer contents agree ([[def-jordan-inner-and-outer-content]]). A **cell particle rule** is a nonempty locally finite family of bounded Jordan-measurable cells $C_j\subseteq\Omega$ whose interiors are disjoint and whose union covers $\Omega$ up to their shared boundaries, together with nodes $x_j\in C_j$ and positive volumes $V_j=\int 1_{C_j}$. The cell volume integral is Riemann-defined and equals the Jordan content ([[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]]). Its fill radius is $h=\sup_j\sup_{y\in C_j}|y-x_j|$, using the Euclidean norm from [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]; require $0<h<\infty$. Assume finite constants $C_V,C_L>0$ satisfy $V_j\le C_Vh^d$ and the local volume bound
$$\sum_{j:C_j\cap B(x,r)\ne\varnothing}V_j\le C_L(r+h)^d$$
This finite partition identity is part of the quadrature data.

source_excerpts: Let $\mathbb C(\lambda)$ denote the field of quotients of complex scalar polynomials. Let $R(\lambda)\in\mathbb C(\lambda)^{n\times n}$ with $n\ge1$ be a square matrix whose entries are rational functions of $\lambda$. Write each entry as a reduced scalar fraction (common polynomial factors have been cancelled), and let $q(\lambda)$ be the monic least common multiple of their denominators. Thus the zero set $\mathcal P:=\{\lambda:q(\lambda)=0\}$ is exactly the set of poles of at least one entry. Define the pole-free domain $\Omega:=\mathbb C\setminus\mathcal P$ and the polynomial matrix $N(\lambda):=q(\lambda)R(\lambda)$, whose entries are polynomials as in [[def-matrix-polynomial-and-homogeneous-eigenpairs]]. A **rational eigenpair** is a pair $(\lambda,x)$ with $\lambda\in\Omega$, $x\in\mathbb C^n\setminus\{0\}$, and $R(\lambda)x=0$; its $\lambda$ is a rational eigenvalue. The **cleared-denominator polynomial equation** is $N(\lambda)x=0$, but it represents the rational eigenproblem only on $\Omega$. Any solution at a pole is an inadmissible candidate, even when the cleared polynomial matrix is singular there.

source_excerpts: Let $a<c<b$ and $f\in C^1([a,b])$. The **symmetric Cauchy principal value** of $f(x)/(x-c)$, when the limit exists, is
$$\operatorname{PV}\!\int_a^b\frac{f(x)}{x-c}\,dx:=\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\left(\int_a^{c-\varepsilon}\frac{f(x)}{x-c}\,dx+\int_{c+\varepsilon}^b\frac{f(x)}{x-c}\,dx\right),$$

$$\operatorname{PV}\!\int_a^b\frac{f(x)}{x-c}\,dx:=\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\left(\int_a^{c-\varepsilon}\frac{f(x)}{x-c}\,dx+\int_{c+\varepsilon}^b\frac{f(x)}{x-c}\,dx\right),$$

where $0<\varepsilon<\min(c-a,b-c)$. [[lem-c1-divided-difference-extends-continuously]] supplies the continuous subtraction remainder; the existence and value of the limit are proved in [[thm-cauchy-principal-value-subtraction-identity]].

source_excerpts: Let $h>0$, let $I_j=[jh,(j+1)h)$, and let $x_{i+1/2}=(i+1)h$. For $u\in C^5$ on the union of cells $I_{i-2},\ldots,I_{i+2}$, let $p_0,p_1,p_2$ be the cell-average functionals in [[def-na-high-resolution-reconstruction]]. Each candidate reproduces every polynomial of degree at most two exactly at $x_{i+1/2}$. The ideal combination $p_{opt}=p_0/10+3p_1/5+3p_2/10$ reproduces every polynomial of degree at most four and satisfies $|p_{opt}-u(x_{i+1/2})|\le (23/15)(3^5/5!)\,\sup|u^{(5)}|\,h^5$. Each candidate separately satisfies $|p_k-u(x_{i+1/2})|\le15\sup|u'''|h^3$.
1.1 Combining the three coefficient vectors in [F1] gives $p_{opt}=(2U_{i-2}-13U_{i-1}+47U_i+27U_{i+1}-3U_{i+2})/60$. [F1, algebra]

3.1 Let $T_4$ be the degree-four Taylor polynomial of $u$ at $x_{i+1/2}$ and put $M_5=\sup|u^{(5)}|$ on the stencil. By [F2], the cell-average remainder after subtracting $T_4$ has magnitude at most $M_5(3h)^5/5!$ in each cell. Step 2.1 reproduces $T_4$ exactly, and the absolute coefficients of $p_{opt}$ sum to $(2+13+47+27+3)/60=23/15$. Therefore $|p_{opt}-u(x_{i+1/2})|\le(23/15)M_5(3h)^5/5!$, as claimed. [F1, F2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

3.1 Let $A$ be any bounded measurable set and let $C$ be a bounded set containing the support of $g$. Polar coordinates show $\sup_{y\in C}\int_A|\Phi_k(x-y)|dx<\infty$, since $A-y$ lies in a fixed-radius ball and $\int_0^R r^{-1}r^2dr<\infty$. Tonelli then gives $\int_A\int_C|\Phi_k(x-y)||g(y)|dy\,dx<\infty$, so the defining convolution is absolutely finite for almost every $x\in A$ and belongs to $L^1(A)$. Step 2.1 translated by $y$ gives $\langle(-\Delta-k^2)V,\varphi\rangle=\int g(y)\varphi(y)\,dy$. source_excerpts: Let $\Omega^-$ be a bounded connected $C^2$ domain in $\mathbb R^3$ with connected boundary $\Gamma$, let $\Omega^+=\mathbb R^3\setminus\overline{\Omega^-}$ be connected, and let $n$ point outward from $\Omega^-$. Fix $k>0$ and $\eta\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$. The outgoing Helmholtz kernel is
$$G_k(x,y)=\frac{e^{ik|x-y|}}{4\pi|x-y|},\qquad x\ne y.$$

For $\phi\in C^\infty(\Gamma)$ and $x\notin\Gamma$, define $S_k\phi(x)=\int_\Gamma G_k(x,y)\phi(y)\,dS_y$ and $D_k\phi(x)=\int_\Gamma\partial_{n_y}G_k(x,y)\phi(y)\,dS_y$. The **combined-field potential** is $u_\phi=D_k\phi-i\eta S_k\phi$, and its exterior trace defines the smooth-density operator $A_{k,\eta}\phi=\gamma^+u_\phi$. This definition makes no assertion that $A_{k,\eta}$ extends boundedly or Fredholmly to a Sobolev space; these analytical properties are proved in separate theorems. For this smooth-boundary branch, $\gamma^+$ denotes the trace from $\Omega^+$ and uses the same fixed normal $n$ as the interior trace. For this $C^2$ surface, fix a finite graph atlas and subordinate partition as in the general Lipschitz chart-space convention of [[def-bem-lipschitz-polyhedral-boundary-and-trace-spaces]], using graph surface measure. Use its square-sum Hilbert norm, real spaces, complexification and conjugate-dual convention for $H^{\pm1/2}(\Gamma)$. This imports the space convention only; the $C^2$ trace/lift and layer theorems are proved separately and do not invoke the polyhedral trace theorem.

source_excerpts: Let $L>0$, odd $N\ge3$, $h=L/N$, and $f\in C^2(\mathbb T_L^d)$ for $d\in\{1,2,3\}$. With the uniform tensor grid $x_j=hj$ and indices taken modulo $N$,
$$ \left|h^d\sum_{j\in(\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z)^d}f(x_j)-\int_{[0,L]^d}f(x)\,dx\right| \le \frac{L^dh^2}{12}\sum_{a=1}^d\|\partial_{aa}f\|_\infty . $$

2.1 For each coordinate $a$, let $Q_a$ denote the periodic trapezoid operator in that coordinate and $I_a$ integration over that coordinate. Both have sup-norm operator bound at most $L$, since their weights are nonnegative and sum to $L$. The telescoping identity $Q_1\cdots Q_d-I_1\cdots I_d =\sum_{a=1}^d Q_1\cdots Q_{a-1}(Q_a-I_a)I_{a+1}\cdots I_d$ holds by cancellation. In the $a$th summand, the one-dimensional bound from step 1.1 applies after the later-coordinate integrations; differentiation in coordinate $a$ commutes with those integrations. The other $d-1$ operators contribute at most $L^{d-1}$ in sup norm. Thus that summand is bounded by $L^dh^2\|\partial_{aa}f\|_\infty/12$. Summing these bounds gives the displayed estimate, because $Q_1\cdots Q_d f=h^d\sum_jf(x_j)$ and $I_1\cdots I_df=\int_{[0,L]^d}f$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

source_excerpts: Assume AC and Countable Choice. In dimension two let $K=\Psi(\widetilde K)$, where $\widetilde K$ is a shape-regular affine triangle of diameter comparable to $h_K$, and $\Psi$ extends to a $C^2$ diffeomorphism on a neighborhood of $\overline{\widetilde K}$. Assume $\|D\Psi\|_\infty+\|D\Psi^{-1}\|_\infty+\|D^2\Psi\|_\infty+\|J_\Psi^{-1}\|_\infty$ are uniformly bounded. Let $v$ denote its continuous representative and set $I_Kv=(I_{\widetilde K}(v\circ\Psi))\circ\Psi^{-1}$, the mapped nodal P1 interpolant. For $v\in H^2(K)$, $\|v-I_Kv\|_{L^2(K)}\le C h_K^2\|v\|_{H^2(K)}$ and $|v-I_Kv|_{H^1(K)}\le C h_K\|v\|_{H^2(K)}$, with $C$ uniform over the family.

1.1 First apply [F4] to $w=v\circ\Psi$ on the interiors of the reference and curved cells. The maps extend to a $C^2$ diffeomorphism on neighborhoods of the compact cell closures, and the stated derivative, inverse-derivative, and Jacobian bounds give $w\in H^2(\widetilde K)$ with $\|w\|_{H^2(\widetilde K)}\le C\|v\|_{H^2(K)}$. Now [F5] supplies the unique continuous representative $\widetilde v$ of $w$ on $\overline{\widetilde K}$, so its three reference-vertex values are defined. The function $\widetilde v\circ\Psi^{-1}$ is continuous on $\overline K$ and represents $v$, by the inverse-composition part of [F4]. If $g$ is any other continuous representative of $v$ on $\overline K$, then $g\circ\Psi$ is a continuous representative of $w$ and equals $\widetilde v$ by [F5]; hence the representative on $K$ is unique. Its values at the curved-cell vertices are exactly the pulled-back nodal values. Applying [F4] to the inverse map also gives the uniform $L^2$ and $H^1$ norm bounds needed when the interpolation error is pushed back to $K$. [F2, F4, F5, given, algebra]

3.1 Push the error through $\Psi^{-1}$ using step 1.1. The resulting uniform norm bounds are the two claimed estimates. AC is used only in the automatic nodal-boundedness clause of [F1], and Countable Choice is used through [F1] and [F4]. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

$$F(\alpha)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-\alpha u^2}\,du$$

4.1 Fix $\lambda>0$ and $\sigma=\pm1$, and for $\varepsilon>0$ set $\alpha=\varepsilon-i\sigma\lambda/2$. For any $\varepsilon\ge0$ and $T>R>0$, [F27] gives the phase derivative and [F28] justifies integration by parts on $[R,T]$. The amplitude derivative is $(e^{-\varepsilon u^2}/u)'=-2\varepsilon e^{-\varepsilon u^2}-e^{-\varepsilon u^2}/u^2$ by [F22]--[F24]; the boundary terms are at most $2/(\lambda R)$. For $\varepsilon>0$, using $u\ge R$ and then [F22], [F23], [F29], and [F36] gives $\int_R^\infty2\varepsilon e^{-\varepsilon u^2}du\le R^{-1}\int_R^\infty2\varepsilon u e^{-\varepsilon u^2}du=e^{-\varepsilon R^2}/R\le1/R$; when $\varepsilon=0$ this derivative term is zero. Also $e^{-\varepsilon u^2}\le1$ by [F33], so $\int_R^\infty e^{-\varepsilon u^2}u^{-2}du\le1/R$. Including the factor $1/\lambda$ gives $|\int_R^T e^{-\varepsilon u^2}e^{i\sigma\lambda u^2/2}du|\le4/(\lambda R)$, and the negative tail has the same bound by $u\mapsto-u$. This is uniform for $\varepsilon\ge0$; on every finite interval the damped integrand converges uniformly as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. Given a tolerance, first choose $R$ so both tails are uniformly small and then pass to the limit on $[-R,R]$; this proves that the Abel limit equals the ordinary two-sided improper integral. As $\varepsilon\downarrow0$, $|\alpha|\to\lambda/2$ and $\arg\alpha\to-\sigma\pi/2$, so step 3.1 gives $\sqrt\pi(\lambda/2)^{-1/2}e^{i\sigma\pi/4}=\sqrt{2\pi/\lambda}e^{i\sigma\pi/4}$. source_excerpts: On $[0,1]^d$, $d\in\{2,3\}$, choose in coordinate $r$ any finite clamped knot vector $\Xi_r=(\xi^{(r)}_i)$ of degree $p_r\ge1$, with interior multiplicity at most $p_r+1$. Let $h_r$ be its maximum positive span length, $B^{(r)}_i$ its canonical degree-$p_r$ basis, and $t^{(r)}_i=p_r^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^{p_r}\xi^{(r)}_{i+k}$ its Greville points. For $g\in C^1([0,1]^d)$ with $M_g$-Lipschitz gradient, define the actual tensor comparison spline
$$\mathcal Sg(x)=\sum_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}g(t^{(1)}_{i_1},\ldots,t^{(d)}_{i_d})\prod_{r=1}^d B^{(r)}_{i_r}(x_r).$$

3.1 At an exterior endpoint of a clamped vector, only its first, respectively last, basis function has value one; the rest are zero. The corresponding Greville point is that endpoint. Substitution into the tensor formula gives exactly the asserted tangential face formula and zero-face preservation. Reflection reverses the knot list and sends each Greville point to $1-t_i$. On open knot cells it reverses the indexed basis functions by the Cox–de Boor recurrence in [F1], starting with the interval indicators. At a fully repeated knot the individual right-cell conventions need not commute with reflection, but the constructed sampled sum is continuous by step 2.1, so equality of the reflected sums on open cells extends to every knot and endpoint. Permuting coordinates merely permutes finite product factors. Consequently aligned face formulas agree under all declared identifications. Constant multiplication commutes with their finite linear sums. [F1, step 2.1, given, algebra] ∎

source_excerpts: Let the planar interface be $x=0$, with constant isotropic media $(\epsilon_i,\mu_i)$ on $x<0$ ($i=1$) and $x>0$ ($i=2$). For angular frequency $\omega>0$, define impedances $\eta_i=\sqrt{\mu_i/\epsilon_i}$ and wave numbers $k_i=\omega\sqrt{\epsilon_i\mu_i}$. Take the real parts of the phasors
$$E_z^-=E_0\left(e^{i(k_1x-\omega t)}+R e^{i(-k_1x-\omega t)}\right),\quad H_y^-=-\frac{E_0}{\eta_1}e^{i(k_1x-\omega t)}+\frac{R E_0}{\eta_1}e^{i(-k_1x-\omega t)},$$

2.1 Solving the first equation for $T$ and substituting into the second gives $\eta_2(1-R)=\eta_1(1+R)$, hence $R=\frac{\eta_2-\eta_1}{\eta_1+\eta_2},\qquad T=\frac{2\eta_2}{\eta_1+\eta_2}.$ Because both fields have only tangential components, their normal traces vanish on both sides, so the normal interface conditions in [F1] also hold. [F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

source_excerpts: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let hybrid meshes in [[def-hybrid-mimetic-fv-scheme]] form a regular simplicial companion family, with cell points equal to volume centroids, and let $0<\underline\alpha\le\alpha_{0,K}\le\overline\alpha<\infty$ uniformly. Let $p>\max(1,2d/(d+2))$, $p'=p/(p-1)$, and let $a$ have precisely the Carathéodory, growth, coercivity and monotonicity hypotheses of [[def-pe12-monotone-diffusion-flux]]. Let $f\in L^{p'}(Q)$, $Q=(0,T)\times\Omega$, and let initial cell states obey $\Pi_hU_h^0\to u_0$ strongly in $H=L^2(\Omega)$. Each finite backward-Euler step in the hybrid Definition has a solution. Initial face values can be set arbitrarily because only initial cell values occur in the time term.
On arbitrary time partitions with maximum step $\delta_h\to0$, every selection of step solutions satisfies, uniformly in $h$,

6.1 Compactness $V\Subset L^p$ and continuous $V\to H$ give for each $\varepsilon>0$ an Ehrling estimate $\|z\|_p\le\varepsilon\|z\|_V+C_\varepsilon\|z\|_H$. Indeed, if this failed, normalize counterexamples to $\|z_j\|_p=1$, with $\|z_j\|_V\le1/\varepsilon$ and $\|z_j\|_H\to0$. Compactness in $L^p$ gives a limit of norm one, while the $H$ convergence makes that limit zero as a distribution, a contradiction. Apply this estimate to $E_h\overline U_h-u$, whose $L^p(V)$ norm is bounded and whose $L^p(H)$ norm tends to zero. It tends to zero in $L^p(Q)$ after $h\to0$ and then $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. Its $L^p(Q)$ distance from $\Pi_h\overline U_h$ is $O(h)$ by [F1]. This proves the remaining strong convergence. All arguments used only $h\to0$ and $\delta_h\to0$ separately. [F1, F3, step 5.1, algebra] ∎

$$Q^0_{\varepsilon,h}f(x)=\sum_jV_jf(x_j)W_\varepsilon(x-x_j),\qquad Q^1_{\varepsilon,h}f(x)=\sum_jV_jf(x_j)\nabla W_\varepsilon(x-x_j).$$

2.1 Put g₁(y)=f(y)∇W_ε(x−y). On any segment y(t)=y₀+t(y₁−y₀), [F6] gives componentwise chain and product rules, and Cauchy-Schwarz [F7] gives ||(g₁∘y)'(t)||₂≤(ε^(−d−1)M₁||∇f||∞+ε^(−d−2)M₂||f||∞)|y₁−y₀| by [F3]. Applying the vector mean value inequality [F5] bounds its Lipschitz constant by this expression. Its support is contained in the same closed ball, so [F2] gives the active-volume bound from step 1.1. Apply [F4] to each vector component; taking the Euclidean norm costs at most a factor √d, and [F4] contributes a factor 2; both are absorbed into C. Cancelling ε^d proves the second inequality. source_excerpts: Consider the one-dimensional interval $0\le x\le L$ with Dirichlet endpoints, source point $x_0=L/2$, and a PML beginning at $x_0$, so $X(x_0)=x_0$ and $X(L)=L+iS$ with $S>0$. For $kL=(2m+1)\pi$, $m\in\mathbb N_0$, the Green function of $-d^2/dX^2-k^2$ at the source has magnitude
$$|G(x_0,x_0)|=\frac{\coth(kS)}{k}\sim\frac1{k^2S}\quad(S\downarrow0).$$

2.1 At $X'=x_0=L/2$, $X_L=L+iS$, and $kL=(2m+1)\pi$, the numerator magnitude is $\cosh(kS)$ and the denominator magnitude is $k\sinh(kS)$; this follows from $\sin((m+1/2)\pi)=(-1)^m$ and $|\sin(n\pi+it)|=\sinh(t)$ for integer $n$ and $t>0$. Hence $|G(x_0,x_0)|=\coth(kS)/k$. Since $\sinh t\sim t$ and $\cosh t\to1$ as $t\downarrow0$, this is asymptotic to $1/(k^2S)$. At $S=0$, $\sin(kL)=0$ and $\sin(kx)$ satisfies both homogeneous Dirichlet conditions, proving resonance. The same damping parameter in [F2] gives round-trip reflected amplitude $e^{-2kS}\to1$, so the growing cavity response accompanies vanishing attenuation. [given, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

source_excerpts: Use [[alg-hlr-bottom-up-recompression]] on a finite factor-sum tree for one admissible block over $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, with exact arithmetic, rank cap $k\ge1$, node tolerances $\theta_v\ge0$, and $\sum_v\theta_v\le\delta_b$. Let $T_v$ be the subtree rooted at $v$, and let $M_v$ be the sum of its exact leaf contributions. Whenever all calls in $T_v$ succeed, the returned factors represent a matrix $\widehat M_v$ of rank at most $k$, and the reported bound satisfies
$$\|M_v-\widehat M_v\|_F\le e_v=\sum_{w\in T_v}\rho_w\le\sum_{w\in T_v}\theta_w.$$

2.1 Suppose $v$ is internal with children $v_1,v_2$. Their exact targets add to $M_v$, and their returned approximations add to the matrix $Z_v$ supplied to the core-SVD call. The Frobenius triangle inequality from [F3,F4] gives $\|M_v-Z_v\|_F\le e_{v_1}+e_{v_2}$. By [F1,F2], $\|Z_v-\widehat M_v\|_F=\rho_v$, hence $\|M_v-\widehat M_v\|_F\le e_{v_1}+e_{v_2}+\rho_v=e_v$. Step 1.1 is the leaf base case; induction over the finite tree proves the root error bound. The recurrence for $e_v$ gives $e_{\rm root}=\sum_{v\in T}\rho_v\le\sum_{v\in T}\theta_v\le\delta_b$. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, induction, algebra] ∎

source_excerpts: Use the dyadic root square $H=[0,4]^2$. Put $P=[0,2]\times[0,2]$ and $Q=[2,4]\times[0,2]$; the other two root children are empty. Within $P$ name its lower-left and lower-right children $C_0=[0,1]\times[0,1]$ and $C=[1,2]\times[0,1]$. Within $Q$ name its lower-left, lower-right, and upper-left children $D_0=[2,3]\times[0,1]$, $D=[3,4]\times[0,1]$, and $D_1=[2,3]\times[1,2]$; its upper-right child is empty. Let the leaf threshold be $s=2$ and split each cell with more than two labels. Put unit charges at $c\pm\tfrac14$ in $C$, where $c=\tfrac32+\tfrac12i$. Put zero-charge labels at $\tfrac12+\tfrac12i$ in $C_0$, $d=\tfrac72+\tfrac12i$ in $D$, $\tfrac52+\tfrac12i$ in $D_0$, and $\tfrac52+\tfrac32i$ in $D_1$. Thus $P$ and $Q$ have three labels each and split; their named children are leaves. In the recursive ordered cell pair $(P,Q)$, splitting the source exposes $(C,Q)$, and then splitting $Q$ exposes the separated pair $(C,D)$. The far difference disk has center $2$ and radius $\sqrt2$, so use its analytic logarithm real at $2$. Take order $p=1$.

1.1 The root has six labels, and its nonempty children $P,Q$ each have three, so threshold $s=2$ makes $H,P,Q$ internal while all named grandchildren are leaves. The centers of $P,Q$ are $1+i,3+i$, their radii are $\sqrt2$, and their center distance is $2<2\sqrt2$, so $(P,Q)$ is not separated. Its equal side lengths make the rule split the source $P$; child $C$ has center $c=3/2+i/2$ and radius $\sqrt2/2$. The pair $(C,Q)$ is not separated because its center distance is $\sqrt{5/2}<3\sqrt2/2$. Splitting the larger cell $Q$ exposes $D$ centered at $d=7/2+i/2$; now $|d-c|=2>\sqrt2/2+\sqrt2/2$. Thus the list recursion records $(C,D)$ as a far pair, and the zero-charge label at $d$ is the target at the target-cell center. [given, F1, algebra]

3.1 For the only far interaction with nonzero source charge, $Q_C=2$, $R=2$, and $\rho=\sqrt2/2\in(1/2,1)$. The [F3] bounds are $\rho^2/(1-\rho)>1/4$ and $\rho/(1-\rho)>1/2$; all other far source cells have $Q_C=0$. Any direct near pairs from the zero-charge labels contribute exactly zero, so the errors in step 2.1 satisfy the theorem's global sums. [given, F3, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

source_excerpts: Input two cyclic vertex lists for positive-area convex polygons in $\mathbb R^2$, with rational coordinates. The closing edge is implicit; if the last listed vertex repeats the first, delete that final copy. Delete consecutive duplicate vertices, including across the cyclic endpoint, then return unresolved if a list has fewer than three vertices, any remaining repeated vertex, a zero-length edge, or zero signed shoelace area. Reverse a negatively oriented list so both polygons are counterclockwise. For each list, certify convexity as follows: for every directed edge, evaluate the orientation of that edge with every listed vertex and require every sign to be nonnegative; if three consecutive vertices are collinear, require the middle one to lie between the other two; and for every pair of nonadjacent closed edges, certify that they do not intersect. Test the latter exactly using the four orientation signs: two segments $AB,CD$ intersect if the signs for $C,D$ against $AB$ are strictly opposite and the signs for $A,B$ against $CD$ are strictly opposite, or if one of these signs is zero and its point lies in the closed coordinatewise bounding rectangle of the corresponding segment. 4.1 Consider any matrix $A$ passed to `ExactSolve`; steps 1.1 and 3.1 show it is real, symmetric, positive definite, and hence nonsingular. After $k-1$ elimination stages its coefficient matrix is row-equivalent to $A$ and has block form $\begin{pmatrix}R&C\\0&S\end{pmatrix}$, where $R$ is upper triangular with nonzero diagonal. The full matrix and $R$ are nonsingular, so $S$ is nonsingular: otherwise a nonzero $z$ with $Sz=0$ and the solution $y$ of $Ry=-Cz$ would give a nonzero kernel vector $(y,z)$. Thus the first column of $S$ has a nonzero entry, and the prescribed least-row search finds a pivot. Row swaps and row additions preserve the solution set; after finitely many stages the system is upper triangular with nonzero diagonal. Back substitution is finite and correct by [F7], so `ExactSolve` terminates without its singular branch and returns the unique solution of the assembled matrix equation. The micro systems in step 1.1 are exactly the restricted cell variational equations on a basis; the macro system in step 3.1 is exactly the macro variational equation on a basis. This proves the solver assertion for both. [F1, step 1.1, step 3.1, F7, algebra] ∎

source_excerpts: For each column $j$, define the mean-zero periodic flux $q^j(y)=a(y)(e_j+\nabla\chi_j(y))-A^*e_j$. There is a mean-zero periodic tensor $\sigma^j\in H^1_\#(Y;\mathbb R^{d\times d})$ such that $\sigma^j_{ik}=-\sigma^j_{ki}$ and
$$q_i^j=\sum_{k=1}^d\partial_{y_k}\sigma^j_{ik}\quad\text{in distributions on the torus},\qquad \|\sigma^j\|_{H^1(Y)}\le C_d\|q^j\|_{L^2(Y)}.$$

2.1 For $m\ne0$ define $\widehat\sigma^j_{ik}(m)=\frac{m_k\widehat q_i^j(m)-m_i\widehat q_k^j(m)}{2\pi i|m|^2},\qquad \widehat\sigma^j_{ik}(0)=0.$ Then $\widehat\sigma^j_{ik}=-\widehat\sigma^j_{ki}$ and $\sum_k2\pi im_k\widehat\sigma^j_{ik}(m)=\widehat q_i^j(m)-\frac{m_i}{|m|^2}\sum_km_k\widehat q_k^j(m)=\widehat q_i^j(m)$ by step 1.1. Also $|\widehat\sigma^j(m)|\le C_d|m|^{-1}|\widehat q^j(m)|$, so $\sum_m(1+|m|^2)|\widehat\sigma^j(m)|^2\le C_d\sum_m|\widehat q^j(m)|^2$. Parseval [F3] gives an $H^1$ periodic tensor with the asserted norm bound and divergence; conjugate symmetry of the coefficients makes it real. [step 1.1, F3, A1, algebra] ∎

2.1 For $m\ne0$ define $\widehat\sigma^j_{ik}(m)=\frac{m_k\widehat q_i^j(m)-m_i\widehat q_k^j(m)}{2\pi i|m|^2},\qquad \widehat\sigma^j_{ik}(0)=0.$ Then $\widehat\sigma^j_{ik}=-\widehat\sigma^j_{ki}$ and $\sum_k2\pi im_k\widehat\sigma^j_{ik}(m)=\widehat q_i^j(m)-\frac{m_i}{|m|^2}\sum_km_k\widehat q_k^j(m)=\widehat q_i^j(m)$ by step 1.1. Also $|\widehat\sigma^j(m)|\le C_d|m|^{-1}|\widehat q^j(m)|$, so $\sum_m(1+|m|^2)|\widehat\sigma^j(m)|^2\le C_d\sum_m|\widehat q^j(m)|^2$. Parseval [F3] gives an $H^1$ periodic tensor with the asserted norm bound and divergence; conjugate symmetry of the coefficients makes it real. [step 1.1, F3, A1, algebra] ∎

source_excerpts: Assume the Axiom of Choice. On each coordinate interval $[0,1]$, let a clamped degree-$p_r$ knot mesh have largest cell size $h_r$, and let $Q_r$ be a family as in [[def-local-spline-quasi-interpolant]] with reproduction order $0\le\ell_r\le p_r$, local constant $M_r$, and stability constant $C_r$. Suppose $g$ belongs to the anisotropic Sobolev class with each pure derivative $\partial_r^{\ell_r+1}g\in L^2(\widehat\Omega)$ and with sections to which the one-dimensional estimate of [[thm-sobolev-spline-quasi-interpolant-rate]] applies almost everywhere. Require each $Q_r$ to have its bounded extension to $L^2(\widehat\Omega)$, acting in coordinate $r$, with norm at most $S_r=C_r\sqrt{M_r}$; require the coordinate operators to commute pairwise and to commute with weak derivatives in every other coordinate on the stated anisotropic class. These are explicit hypotheses on the supplied family, not conclusions of the univariate rate theorem. Under the Axiom of Choice, completed-product Fubini is available and the sectionwise operators and derivatives are measurable. Define $\mathcal Q:=Q_d\cdots Q_1$ and set $A_r:=(1+C_r)M_r^{\ell_r+1+1/2}/\ell_r!$. Then $\mathcal Qg$ is in the tensor-product spline numerator space and
$$\|g-\mathcal Qg\|_{L^2(\widehat\Omega)} \le\sum_{r=1}^d A_r\!\left(\prod_{j\ne r}S_j\right)h_r^{\ell_r+1}\|\partial_r^{\ell_r+1}g\|_{L^2(\widehat\Omega)}.$$

3.1 By [F4], $\mathcal Qg/W$ is a NURBS analysis function. Its physical push-forward differs from $u$ by $(g-\mathcal Qg)/W$ composed with $F^{-1}$. Since $W\ge w_-$, its parametric $L^2$ norm is at most $w_-^{-1}\|g-\mathcal Qg\|_2$; applying [F5] proves the physical $L^2$ bound. No gradient estimate is used, so no energy-norm conclusion follows. [F4, F5, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

For $z\in K$ and $q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}$, put $P(z,q)$ when the set-defined upper and lower envelopes in [F2] give $$|V_k(y)-u(z)|\le\varepsilon/3\quad\text{for every integer }k\text{ with }1/k<q \text{ and every }y\text{ with }|y-z|<q,$$ and continuity gives $|u(y)-u(z)|<\varepsilon/3$ whenever $|y-z|<q$. The family of all balls $$\{B(z,q/2):z\in K,\ q\in\mathbb Q_{>0},\ P(z,q)\}$$ covers $K$: each point has a positive real radius from the two envelope definitions and continuity, and a smaller rational radius still works. This is the family of all qualifying pairs, so no radius is selected for every point. By [F8] take a finite subcover and let $q_*>0$ be its least radius. For $1/k<q_*$, every $y\in K$ lies in one of these balls and therefore $|V_k(y)-u(y)|<2\varepsilon/3<\varepsilon$. This proves uniform convergence on the fundamental box through $T'$, hence on the torus and every compact subset of $\mathbb T^d\times[0,T)$. [F2, F8, step 2.3, algebra] ∎

Its output tetrahedra cover the convex hull, meet in common faces, and have empty power spheres in the original weak sense. In the zero-weight case they are ordinary Delaunay tetrahedra. The algorithm reports every coplanar four-site base as `degenerate-base` and makes no tetrahedralization claim on the lower-dimensional branch.

source_excerpts: On a periodic three-dimensional Yee grid choose one oriented $x$-edge $e_0$ from vertex $v_0$ to a distinct vertex $v_1$ (choose at least two cells in the periodic $x$ direction), set $j^{1/2}=J\mathbf e_0$ with $J\ne0$, and set every other current cochain to zero. Let $S=0$, initialize $G^TM_ee^0=\rho^0$, and keep the charge row fixed at $\rho^1=\rho^0$. This charge choice violates the discrete continuity equation because $G^Tj^{1/2}\ne0$.

1.1 Apply $G^T$ to the electric row in [F1]. Since $G^TC^T=(CG)^T=0$ and the initial Gauss relation holds, this gives $G^TM_ee^1-\rho^1=-\Delta t\,G^Tj^{1/2}=-\Delta t J G^T\mathbf e_0.$ By [F2], the residual is $+\Delta t J$ at $v_0$, $-\Delta t J$ at $v_1$, and zero at the other vertices. It is nonzero because $J\ne0$. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 If instead the charge were updated by $\rho^1=\rho^0-\Delta t G^Tj^{1/2}$, the same calculation would give $G^TM_ee^1-\rho^1=0$. The drift is therefore exactly the discrete-continuity defect. [F1, given, algebra] ∎

$$X_h=\{v_h\in V_h:(v_h,\nabla q_h)_{L^2}=0\text{ for every }q_h\in S_h\}.$$

4.1 In general topology $B\subset K$ and $B_h\subset K_h$. Closedness of $B$ gives $K=B\oplus\mathcal H$, while finite-dimensional orthogonal decomposition gives $K_h=B_h\oplus\mathcal H_h$ and $Z_h=X_h\cap\mathcal H_h^\perp$. The unit ball of $\mathcal H$ is graph bounded and lies in $B^\perp$; [F2] and [F4] make it relatively compact by the argument in step 1.1. Nonzero $a_h\in\mathcal H_h$ has $\|a_h\|_2>0$ but curl zero, disproving a curl Poincare bound on all $X_h$ whenever such a mode exists. Steps 1.1 and 2.1 still prove compactness of $X_h$ and step 2.2 proves the quotient inequality. source_excerpts: For every tolerance $0<\tau\le\sigma/4=1/4$, the algorithm [[alg-delaunay-seeded-curved-uniform-nvb-refinement]] with square boundary angle $\alpha=\pi/2$ and nonincident-feature separation $\sigma=1$ terminates after finitely many three-generation cycles. Its reference triangles remain right isosceles with minimum angle $\pi/4$, all interfaces match, and every curved cell map is orientation preserving. Pointwise on each cell, if $a_K$ is an affine parametrization of its reference triangle, then the induced metric $G_{\Phi,K}=(D(\Phi\circ a_K))^TD(\Phi\circ a_K)$ has spectral condition number $\kappa_2(G_{\Phi,K})\le(81/16)\kappa_2(G_{\mathrm{ref},K})$, where $G_{\mathrm{ref},K}=(Da_K)^TDa_K$. The returned maximum curved-cell diameter is at most $\tau$. This is a guarantee for this square/shear family; it asserts no general Delaunay minimum-angle theorem, adaptive complexity bound, or 3D shape bound.

1.1 Directly from the square coordinates, each interior angle is $\pi/2$, opposite edges and nonincident vertices/edges are separated by distance $2$, so $\sigma=1$ is a valid lower certificate [A1]. The four corners are distinct dyadic sites in convex position. By [F1] the returned Delaunay triangulation covers the square; with four extreme vertices it has exactly two triangles sharing one diagonal. Each is right isosceles. Labeling the shared diagonal as reference on both sides gives compatible initial labels. [F1, A1, given, algebra]

3.1 Let $A_K=Da_K$. The bounds in step 1.3 imply $\kappa_2(D\Phi)\le\|D\Phi\|_{op}\|D\Phi^{-1}\|_{op}\le9/4$. Since $D(\Phi\circ a_K)=D\Phi(a_K)A_K$, submultiplicativity gives $\kappa_2(D(\Phi\circ a_K))\le(9/4)\kappa_2(A_K)$. The spectral condition number of $D(\Phi\circ a_K)^TD(\Phi\circ a_K)$ is the square of that derivative condition number, and $\kappa_2(A_K^TA_K)=\kappa_2(A_K)^2$, proving the stated $81/16$ metric bound. The reference triangles have disjoint interiors in a square of area $4$. Any right-isosceles reference triangle of diameter at least $\tau/(3/2)$ has area at least $\tau^2/9$; disjoint interiors therefore allow at most $36/\tau^2$ such cells. This packing bound is consistent with the finite uniform refinement and the stated positive feature and angle certificates. [F2, F5, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 1.3, algebra] ∎

$$E_1=(0,0,\sin(\pi x)\sin(2\pi y)),\qquad E_2=(0,0,\sin(2\pi x)\sin(\pi y))$$

3.1 Apply [F2] to the full eigenspace cluster: exactly its actual multiplicity of discrete eigenvalues converges to this value and the discrete eigenspaces converge in gap. The explicit two orthogonal modes show the multiplicity is at least two; no individual basis vector is selected by the theorem. [F2, F4, step 2.1, step 1.3] ∎
